name: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain
summary: A sprain or tear of the medial collateral ligament from a valgus force, usually a blow to the outside of the knee. Most isolated tears, even complete ones, heal well with early functional rehabilitation.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Grade I ~2 weeks; grade II 3–4 weeks; grade III 6–8+ weeks

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Mean lay-off 23 days in professional football

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Valgus stress at 30° (pain and laxity together: LR+ 6.4 with history)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Usually clinical; MRI if laxity in extension or suspected ACL, meniscal or posteromedial injury

keyFacts.label: Mechanism
keyFacts.value: ~70% contact: a blow to the lateral knee

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Most common knee ligament injury in professional football

overview:
The medial collateral ligament (MCL) complex is the primary restraint to valgus stress at the knee and the most commonly injured knee ligament [r1,r2]. Most sprains are caused by a direct blow to the outer side of the knee that forces it into valgus, often with some external rotation of the tibia.

Unlike the cruciate ligaments, the MCL is extra-articular and well vascularised, so it heals with a bridging scar. Isolated injuries of all grades, including complete grade III tears, are managed non-operatively with bracing as needed and early functional rehabilitation, with good long-term results [r1,r11,r12]. The physiotherapist's key tasks are to grade the injury, screen for combined ACL, meniscal and posteromedial corner injury (laxity in full extension is a warning sign), and guide a progressive return to sport (RTS) that typically takes 2–8 weeks [r2,r3].

epidemiology.text: In 27 professional European football teams followed for 11 seasons, MCL injury occurred at 0.33 per 1000 player-hours, nine times more often in matches than in training, and was the most common knee ligament injury; about 70% were contact-related and the average lay-off was 23 days [r2]. In a US military academy cohort, the incidence of isolated MCL sprain was about 7.3 per 1000 person-years, with the highest rates in wrestling, judo, ice hockey and rugby. Male intercollegiate athletes had about 2.6 times the rate of females per athlete-exposure, and grade 1 injuries lost a median of 13.5 days versus 29 days for higher grades [r3].

intrinsic: Male sex (about 2.6–2.9 times the rate of females in intercollegiate athletes) [r3]
Previous MCL injury (reinjury occurs, although lay-off is similar to index injuries) [r2]
Valgus knee alignment and poor neuromuscular control (expert opinion; potentially modifiable)
extrinsic: Contact and collision sports, especially wrestling, judo, ice hockey and rugby [r3]
Match play rather than training (about nine times the rate) [r2]
Tackles and player-to-player contact to the lateral knee [r2]
Skiing in a snow-plough position (valgus and external rotation)

mechanism.summary: The typical mechanism is a valgus force: a blow to the lateral side of the knee, or a fall or tackle onto it, with the foot planted and the knee slightly flexed (about 20–30°), where the superficial MCL is the dominant restraint [r1,r4]. External rotation of the tibia often accompanies the valgus load and adds stress to the deep MCL and posteromedial structures. Non-contact valgus-rotation injuries (cutting, skiing) also occur, and higher-energy or more extended-knee injuries may involve the ACL [r1].
sequence: The athlete's right foot is planted with the knee slightly flexed (about 20–30°) and weight on the leg.
An opponent or the ground strikes the lateral side of the knee, or the lower leg is forced outward.
The knee is driven into valgus in the frontal plane, opening the medial joint line; the tibia often rotates externally.
The superficial MCL, the main restraint to valgus at 20–30° of flexion, tightens and takes the load [r4].
Fibres fail, most often near the femoral attachment or in mid-substance; the deep MCL and posterior oblique ligament may also tear.
With greater force or a straighter knee, the ACL and posteromedial corner fail too, and the lateral compartment may be compressed (bone bruise).
The athlete feels sharp medial pain and may continue briefly; localised medial swelling develops.

variants.name: Contact valgus blow
variants.description: A tackle or collision to the lateral knee with the foot fixed. About 70% of MCL injuries in professional football are contact-related [r2].

variants.name: Non-contact valgus–external rotation
variants.description: Cutting or pivoting with the knee collapsing into valgus and the tibia externally rotated. This may produce combined ACL and MCL injury.

variants.name: Skiing
variants.description: The ski tips separate in a snow-plough position, forcing the knee into valgus and external rotation; MCL sprains are common in recreational skiers.

variants.name: Wrestling and judo
variants.description: Throws and takedowns load the knee into valgus; these sports have among the highest MCL injury rates [r3].

anatomy.text: The medial side of the knee has three main stabilisers. The superficial MCL runs from just proximal and posterior to the medial femoral epicondyle to a broad tibial insertion about 6 cm below the joint line, deep to the pes anserinus. The deep MCL is a thickening of the medial capsule with meniscofemoral and meniscotibial parts attached to the medial meniscus. The posterior oblique ligament reinforces the posteromedial capsule and is tight in extension [r1]. The superficial MCL is the primary restraint to valgus, particularly at 20–30° of flexion; in full extension the posteromedial capsule and cruciates contribute more, so laxity in extension implies a more extensive injury [r1,r4]. The MCL is extra-articular and well vascularised, which explains its good healing capacity.

structures.name: Superficial MCL
structures.role: Primary restraint to valgus (most at 20–30° flexion) and a restraint to external rotation [r1,r4]

structures.name: Deep MCL (meniscofemoral and meniscotibial ligaments)
structures.role: Secondary valgus restraint; anchors the medial meniscus

structures.name: Posterior oblique ligament / posteromedial capsule
structures.role: Restrains valgus and internal rotation near extension [r1]

structures.name: ACL
structures.role: Secondary valgus restraint, particularly near extension; often injured in higher-energy valgus injuries

structures.name: Medial meniscus
structures.role: Attached to the deep MCL; may be injured with it

structures.name: Pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus)
structures.role: Dynamic medial support; lies superficial to the tibial MCL insertion

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Valgus load elongates the superficial MCL beyond its linear range and fibres fail sequentially, from microscopic disruption (grade I) through partial tearing (grade II) to complete loss of continuity (grade III). Tears are most common near the femoral attachment or in the mid-substance; tibial-sided tears heal less predictably, and a torn distal end displaced superficial to the pes anserinus tendons may not heal without surgery [r13].

Because the MCL is extra-articular and well vascularised, the haematoma forms a fibrin clot that is organised into a bridging scar. This scar restores continuity but remains biologically and mechanically inferior to normal ligament for many months: collagen fibrils are smaller, cross-links are immature, and the matrix contains 'flaws', so the healed ligament is weaker and may creep [r5,r6]. Controlled motion and loading during healing improve its organisation and strength, which is the rationale for early functional rehabilitation rather than rigid immobilisation [r6,r12].

structures.name: Superficial MCL
structures.effect: Grade I–III tear, usually femoral or mid-substance; heals with a bridging scar [r1,r5]

structures.name: Deep MCL and posterior oblique ligament
structures.effect: Torn in higher-grade injuries; involvement of the posteromedial corner causes laxity in extension and anteromedial rotatory instability [r1]

structures.name: ACL
structures.effect: Concomitant rupture in higher-energy valgus–rotation injuries; check Lachman in every grade II–III MCL

structures.name: Medial meniscus
structures.effect: Peripheral or meniscocapsular tear through the deep MCL attachment

structures.name: Lateral compartment
structures.effect: Compression bone bruise from the valgus load (contrecoup)

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition from pain and any effusion causes lag and early atrophy, particularly of vastus medialis [r7].

muscles.name: Hamstrings and pes anserinus muscles
muscles.effect: Protective guarding; the knee is often held in slight flexion to unload the MCL.

muscles.name: Hip abductors and external rotators
muscles.effect: Disuse weakness; poor proximal control increases dynamic valgus when the athlete returns to cutting.

cellular.description: Bleeding forms a fibrin clot. Platelets release growth factors, neutrophils and then macrophages clear damaged tissue, and local oedema and pain peak.
Fibroblasts and new capillaries fill the gap with disorganised, predominantly type III collagen, bridging the torn ends [r5].
Collagen realigns along the line of load and matures, but the scar keeps smaller fibrils, immature cross-links and lower strength than native ligament for a long time [r6].

systems.effect: Pain and effusion inhibit quadriceps activation through spinal reflex pathways (arthrogenic muscle inhibition) [r7]. Loss of ligament mechanoreceptor input temporarily reduces joint position sense.
A localised inflammatory response drives the clot-to-scar sequence; effusion is usually small unless intra-articular structures are also injured.
Patients avoid valgus and rotational loads, shortening stance on the injured side and reducing cutting toward the injured side.
Most athletes return quickly, but fear of re-injury can limit tackling and cutting; graded exposure in late rehab helps.

grading.system: Clinical grading (valgus stress at 30° flexion, opening compared with the other side)

grades.description: Localised tenderness; pain on valgus stress but no increased opening (roughly 0–5 mm) and a firm end-feel.
grades.prognosis: Return to sport in about 2 weeks [r3]

grades.description: Partial tear. Increased opening (roughly 5–10 mm) with a firm end point at 30°; stable in full extension.

Complete tear. Opening greater than about 10 mm with a soft or absent end point; on stress radiographs >3.2 mm side-to-side gapping at 20° suggests a complete superficial MCL tear [r9]. Laxity in full extension indicates posteromedial or cruciate involvement.
grades.prognosis: Isolated grade III: non-operative, about 6–8 weeks; combined injuries need surgical review [r1,r13]

timeframes.summary: The MCL heals with a bridging scar. Pain and laxity settle over weeks, but the scar keeps maturing for many months, so strength and neuromuscular control must be rebuilt before full contact.

healing.description: Clot formation, inflammatory cell influx, peak pain and swelling
Fibroblasts lay down type III collagen bridging the tear; protected, progressive loading
Scar matures and aligns; strength remains below normal for months

milestones.label: Return to sport, grade I (median)
milestones.note: Median 13.5 days in a military academy cohort [r3]

milestones.label: Return to sport, grade II–III (median)
milestones.note: Higher grades lost a median of 29 days [r3]

milestones.label: Return to sport, isolated grade III (typical upper range)
Brace discontinued for contact (grade III, typical)

timeframes.returnToSport: Grade I usually within about 2 weeks, grade II–III a median of about 4 weeks, with an average lay-off of 23 days in professional football [r2,r3]. In elite soccer players, 71% returned at the same level after a median of 33 days and reinjury was uncommon [r14]. Progression is criteria-based.

symptoms: Medial knee pain after a blow to the outside of the knee or a valgus twist
Localised swelling over the medial knee; large rapid effusion suggests an intra-articular injury
Pain on cutting toward the opposite side, pushing off, and stairs
A feeling of medial 'opening' or instability in higher grades
signs: Tenderness along the MCL, most often at the femoral attachment near the medial epicondyle
Pain (grade I) or increased opening (grade II–III) on valgus stress at 30° flexion
Minimal to small effusion when isolated
Loss of terminal extension and painful end-range flexion
Antalgic gait with the knee held slightly flexed

subjective: Mechanism: contact to the lateral knee (valgus) versus non-contact pivot (consider ACL)
Location of pain and whether the athlete could continue
Time course of swelling: rapid tense swelling within hours suggests haemarthrosis and an intra-articular injury
Locking, catching or giving way (meniscal tear or ACL injury)
Previous knee injuries; sport, position and competition schedule
observation: Gait: shortened stance, knee held flexed
palpation: Trace the MCL from the femoral origin to the tibial insertion and note the most tender point (femoral, mid-substance or tibial)
Medial joint line (meniscus) versus ligament tenderness
Effusion grading with the stroke test
rangeOfMotion: Terminal extension and end-range flexion are painful
A springy block to extension suggests a displaced meniscal fragment
strength: Quadriceps and hamstring strength once pain allows
Hip abductor and external rotator strength
functional: Hop tests and cutting drills in late rehab

specialTests.name: Valgus stress test at 30° flexion
specialTests.purpose: Isolate the superficial MCL and grade the sprain
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine, thigh supported, knee flexed 20–30°. Stabilise the lateral knee and apply a valgus force at the ankle; compare opening and end-feel with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Medial pain (grade I) or increased opening (grade II–III). In general practice, adding pain and laxity on valgus stress at 30° to history raised the positive likelihood ratio for an MCL lesion to 6.4.
specialTests.lrPositive: 2.3 for pain on valgus stress at 30° alone; 6.4 combined with history and laxity

specialTests.name: Valgus stress test in full extension
specialTests.purpose: Screen for posteromedial corner and cruciate involvement
specialTests.procedure: As above with the knee fully extended.
specialTests.positive: Opening in full extension indicates injury beyond the superficial MCL (posterior oblique ligament, capsule and/or cruciate) and warrants MRI and surgical review [r1].

specialTests.name: Lachman test
specialTests.procedure: Knee at 20–30° flexion; translate the tibia anteriorly while stabilising the femur.
specialTests.positive: Increased anterior translation with a soft end point.

specialTests.name: Anteromedial drawer (Slocum) test
specialTests.purpose: Anteromedial rotatory instability from posteromedial corner injury
specialTests.procedure: Knee at 90° with the tibia externally rotated about 15°; draw the tibia anteriorly.
specialTests.positive: Excess anterior translation of the medial tibial plateau compared with the other side.

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa knee rules
clinicalRules.description: Use to decide on radiographs after acute knee trauma; pooled sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.49 for fracture in adults [r10].

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain, symptoms, function, sport and quality of life

outcomeMeasures.name: Hop test battery
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective limb symmetry before return to sport

imaging.indication: Ottawa rules positive, or adolescent with suspected physeal injury
imaging.findings: Usually normal; bony avulsion; distal femoral physeal fracture in skeletally immature athletes; Pellegrini–Stieda calcification in chronic injury

imaging.indication: Grade III or laxity in extension, suspected ACL/meniscal injury, or failure to progress
imaging.findings: Location and grade of the tear, deep MCL and posterior oblique ligament involvement, displacement of the distal MCL superficial to the pes anserinus, associated ACL, meniscal and bone bruise injuries [r13]

imaging.indication: Objective grading of complete or combined medial injuries
imaging.findings: >3.2 mm side-to-side medial gapping at 20° suggests a complete superficial MCL tear; about 9.8 mm suggests complete medial-sided injury [r9]

differentials.name: ACL rupture (often combined)
differentials.distinguishing: Non-contact pivot, 'pop', rapid haemarthrosis and a positive Lachman. Check every grade II–III MCL for a combined ACL tear.

differentials.name: Medial meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Joint-line rather than ligament tenderness, delayed effusion and mechanical symptoms (locking or catching).

differentials.name: Lateral patellar dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Medial pain from MPFL tearing and medial retinacular tenderness, with a haemarthrosis and a positive apprehension test.

differentials.name: Pes anserine tendinopathy / bursitis
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual onset, tenderness below the joint line over the pes anserinus, and no valgus laxity.

differentials.name: Tibial plateau fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Higher-energy valgus load in an older patient, unable to weight-bear, positive Ottawa rules (lateral plateau fracture with medial ligament injury).

differentials.name: Distal femoral physeal fracture (adolescents)
differentials.distinguishing: In skeletally immature athletes, valgus stress may separate the physis rather than tear the MCL; tenderness is at the physis and radiographs are needed.

redFlags: Gross laxity in more than one plane, or valgus opening in full extension with a positive Lachman or posterior drawer: suspect a multiligament injury or knee dislocation. Check distal pulses and refer the same day.
Rapid tense haemarthrosis within a few hours: suspect intra-articular injury (ACL, osteochondral fracture, patellar dislocation). Refer for MRI and orthopaedic review.
A knee locked in flexion that cannot be extended: suspect a displaced meniscal tear. Arrange urgent orthopaedic review.
Bony tenderness, inability to weight-bear or tenderness over the physis in an adolescent: arrange radiographs to exclude fracture.
Calf pain and swelling after immobilisation or bracing: assess for deep vein thrombosis.

management.principles: Isolated MCL injuries of every grade are managed non-operatively first, with a consensus that this includes acute isolated grade III tears and grade III tears combined with an ACL tear (where the MCL is usually allowed to heal before any ACL reconstruction) [r1]. Early functional rehabilitation with a hinged brace for higher grades gives outcomes comparable with surgery or immobilisation while allowing a faster return to sport [r11,r12]. Surgery is reserved for specific situations: a distal MCL displaced superficial to the pes anserinus (Stener-like lesion), intra-articular entrapment or bony avulsion, severe valgus alignment, persistent valgus instability after rehabilitation, and complex multiligament injuries [r13]. Load is progressed by symptoms, laxity and function rather than fixed timeframes.

medical.name: Hinged knee brace (grade II–III)
medical.description: A hinged brace that resists valgus but allows flexion and extension, worn for about 3–6 weeks depending on grade and sometimes during early return to contact [r12].

medical.name: Analgesia and short-term NSAIDs
medical.description: Simple analgesia and short NSAID courses for pain in the first days. Some concern exists that NSAIDs may impair early ligament healing; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.

medical.name: Surgical repair or reconstruction
medical.description: Indicated for distal MCL displaced over the pes anserinus, intra-articular entrapment or bony avulsion, severe valgus malalignment, chronic valgus instability and complex combined injuries. Primary repair is usually done within 7–10 days [r13].

medical.name: Rigid immobilisation in a cast
medical.description: Prolonged immobilisation produces outcomes no better than functional bracing and causes stiffness and atrophy; it is no longer routinely recommended [r11,r12].

physio.name: Early functional rehabilitation
physio.description: Early range of motion, quadriceps activation, weight-bearing as tolerated and progressive resistance once about 90° of flexion is present, with return to sport on recovery. In athletes with isolated grade III tears this gave good to excellent results at 5 years [r12].

physio.name: Progressive strengthening and neuromuscular training
physio.description: Quadriceps, hamstring and hip strengthening, then single-leg control, landing and cutting drills. Controlled loading during healing improves scar organisation [r6].

physio.name: Strategies for quadriceps inhibition
physio.description: Cryotherapy, compression and NMES alongside exercise in the first 1–2 weeks to reduce arthrogenic muscle inhibition [r7].

physio.name: Graded valgus and rotational loading
physio.description: Avoid valgus stress (side-stepping toward the injured side, breaststroke kick, contact) until a firm end point and pain-free valgus stress testing return, then reintroduce deliberately.

physio.name: Prophylactic knee bracing on return
physio.description: Evidence for prophylactic braces to prevent knee ligament injury is inconsistent, with some studies showing risk reduction and others increased risk [r15]. A functional brace may be considered for early return to contact after grade II–III injury.

education: The MCL is outside the joint and has a good blood supply, so it heals with scar tissue, even when completely torn.
Most people return to sport in 2–8 weeks depending on the grade. Moving and loading the knee early helps the ligament heal stronger.
Wear the brace as advised for higher-grade tears and avoid sideways stress on the knee until your physio clears it.
Rapid swelling, locking or the knee giving way suggest another injury, so report these.
Strength and control around the hip and knee help protect against reinjury.

rehab.overview: Early functional rehabilitation is the standard [r12]. Progress through stages by criteria: pain, swelling, valgus stress findings, range, strength and function. Grade I injuries may complete the program in about 2 weeks; grade III injuries take 6–8 weeks or more and use a hinged brace through stages 1–2. If the ACL is also torn, the MCL is usually rehabilitated first and the ACL pathway then follows.

stages.name: Protect & mobilise
goals: Restore full extension and flexion toward 90°+
Weight-bearing as tolerated (brace for grade II–III)
precautions: Hinged brace as prescribed for grade II–III

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets
exercises.cues: Tighten the thigh and straighten the knee fully

stages.name: Strength & control
goals: Build quadriceps, hamstring and hip strength
precautions: Keep loads in the sagittal plane; avoid valgus and rotation
Progress if no increase in medial pain or laxity the next day

exercises.name: Squat (to box, progressing depth)
exercises.cues: Knees track over the second toe

progressionCriteria: No pain on valgus stress at 30° (or firm end point)
Single-leg squat to 60° without valgus collapse

stages.name: Power, running & agility
precautions: Introduce lateral movements gradually: shuffles before cuts
Consider a functional brace for early frontal-plane drills after grade II–III

exercises.name: Running progression and lateral shuffles
exercises.dosage: Every second day, progressing speed and direction

stages.name: Return to sport
precautions: Graded exposure to tackling and contact
progressionCriteria: Full, pain-free range and no effusion
Shared decision with athlete and staff

criteria: Full, pain-free range of motion and no effusion
No pain and a firm end point on valgus stress at 30°
Quadriceps and hamstring strength ≥ 90% of the other side
Hop test battery ≥ 90% symmetry with good valgus control
Pain-free full-speed running, cutting and sport-specific drills
Completion of full training including contact
tests: Single, triple and crossover hop tests

prognosis: The prognosis for isolated MCL injury is very good. Non-operative treatment of complete tears produces results comparable with surgery or immobilisation, and athletes treated with early functional rehabilitation had mean Hospital for Special Surgery knee scores of 45.9/50 at about 5 years [r11,r12]. In professional football the mean lay-off is 23 days, and reinjuries have a similar lay-off to index injuries [r2]. Among elite European soccer players, 71% returned at the same level, reinjury occurred in 3% and later performance was not reduced [r14]. Outcomes are worse when the injury is combined with ACL or posteromedial corner damage, when the distal MCL is displaced over the pes anserinus, or when valgus instability persists, which can lead to secondary ACL dysfunction and osteoarthritis [r13].
prevention: Neuromuscular training that improves landing and cutting control is reasonable, although MCL-specific prevention trials are lacking.
Prophylactic knee braces have inconsistent effects on knee ligament injury in football and cannot be routinely recommended [r15].
Enforcing rules against tackles to the side of the planted leg (expert opinion).
clinicalPearls: Test valgus at both 30° and full extension. Opening at 30° only is an MCL injury; opening in extension means the posteromedial corner or a cruciate is also torn.
A large, rapid effusion is not typical of an isolated MCL sprain. Look for an ACL, meniscal or osteochondral injury.
Find the most tender point. Femoral-sided tears heal reliably; tibial-sided grade III tears deserve an MRI to exclude displacement over the pes anserinus.
In adolescents, 'MCL' tenderness at the level of the distal femoral physis may be a physeal fracture. X-ray before stressing hard.
Early motion is treatment. The MCL scar organises better under controlled load than in a cast [r6,r12].

captions.text: A soccer player plants the right foot to shield the ball.
An opponent slides in from the outside, aiming at the ball.
The tackle strikes the lateral knee while the foot is fixed and the knee slightly bent.
The knee is forced into valgus: the medial side opens and the MCL is stretched.
Sharp medial knee pain; the player falls but may get up and try to continue.
Zooming into the right knee from the front; the medial side is on the right of the screen.

actions.text: Grade II tear near the femoral attachment

captions.text: The MCL runs from the medial femoral epicondyle to the tibia, about 6 cm below the joint line.
The blow to the outside of the knee opens the medial joint line.
Fibres fail near the femoral attachment: a partial (grade II) tear with a firm end point.
The MCL lies outside the joint, so swelling is local and effusion is usually small.
The lateral compartment may be squeezed, bruising the bone.
Its rich blood supply lets the MCL heal across the gap with scar tissue.
Healthy ligament: crimped type I collagen fibres aligned along the line of load.
Valgus load straightens the crimp and stretches the fibres.
Beyond the elastic range, fibrils slide and start to fail.
Fibres rupture. Full failure is shown; many MCL sprains are partial.
Torn vessels bleed and a fibrin clot fills the gap.
Neutrophils, then macrophages, clear debris and release growth factors.
Fibroblasts bridge the gap with disorganised type III collagen and new capillaries.
With graded loading the scar aligns along the line of load, though it stays weaker for months.
